findings.gate: Universe Bible — Tide Path standing rule / Craft Core authority ladder / THE_AUTHOR Gate 27

draft_evidence.quote: She had not asked. She had come across the camp from the mule with the roll on her back and had put two fingers on his wrist, and then the flat hand on the ribs, on the left, low, where it went, and gone in, and come out, and looked at him as she had looked at a knee.

comparison_evidence.quote: **Cael's Tide-adjacent fragment (B7 Ch13):** partial; Iron; self and contact; the first fragment that does nothing in a fight; engagement field *clinical*; **the standing rule, in Oryn's hand and his: ask first, every time.** Consistent with B2's "Tide-adjacent" anomaly label and Book 15's "Oryn's Tide Path burns out."

findings.consequence: The manuscript explicitly negates consent immediately before Oryn uses contact and current to read Cael's injury. The higher-authority system rule makes asking mandatory in Oryn's hand every time, and the packet requires the reading but does not grant an exception. Because the covenant defines the ethics of this capability and Oryn's care, the scene cannot safely advance while it depicts the breach as ordinary competent conduct.
findings.repair_target: Lines 23-27: preserve the required rib reading and its fixed dialogue, but establish Cael's consent before Oryn goes in; do not treat the existing standing term as a substitute for the every-time ask unless canon is explicitly amended.

findings.gate: Craft Core reader-trust invariant 3 / Voice Charter §3.1 and §5.5

draft_evidence.quote: He could not sleep, and he had known he would not, and he had a reason for not sleeping that was not the ribs and not the stone at the mouth, and he sat up with it against the mule's pack, with the fire low and eleven people asleep or pretending, and Lira awake, across the fire, as she was always awake, looking at nothing.

comparison_evidence.quote: Eleven, and a mule. He entered the count. It was the first time all year that the count had gone the other way. He had counted up at every halt since a landing in the snow — five, six, twelve — and had thought of the counting as a thing that went one way, as a ledger's lines do, and it did not, and he had known that in the abstract for five years and had it now in the particular, and the particular was a boy with a pack too big for him.

findings.consequence: The living company is eleven total after the young one's death. With Cael and Lira both awake, only nine other people can be asleep or pretending; the sentence instead supplies eleven sleepers plus Lira plus Cael. The contradiction lands inside a chapter whose emotional and voice logic depends on exact counting, so a reader is likely to notice the dead apparently restored by arithmetic.
findings.repair_target: Line 45: reconcile the sleepers/pretenders with the established eleven-person total while preserving Cael and Lira awake across the fire.

findings.category: continuity and packet fidelity — Cleon's warning
findings.gate: Packet must_include: Cleon's warning verbatim / Craft Core continuity persistence

draft_evidence.quote:
And Cleon, in a door, with a key in his hand and the lamp behind him, had said the thing that had leaned.

*If that fragment ever reads something for you that shouldn't be made and reads it anyway. Don't tell me. Don't tell anyone. Just remember I said it.*

comparison_evidence.quote:
Cleon had a cup on the table. He had had it there all week — water, from the spring at the gallery's head, in a clay cup that had been a cup for thirty years — and he had not once, in Cael's seeing, drunk from it while he read, because a man who reads with his whole attention does not have a hand to spare for a cup. He picked it up now, and drank.

"I'm going to pretend you didn't tell me that," he said, "for your sake, not mine. But I'll tell you one thing for free, since you can apparently take my whole trade by watching me work it for a minute." He set down the cup. "Everything I read is *made*. Stone, ink, seal — somebody built it, so I can see how. If that fragment ever reads something for you that shouldn't be *made* and reads it anyway — " He stopped. "Don't tell me. Don't tell anyone. Just remember I said it."

He went back to the carving.

findings.consequence: Chapter 13 places the warning at Cleon's table with a cup and stops the sentence at the dash before he resumes. Chapter 22 relocates it to a doorway with a key and turns the interruption into a period. The words mostly survive, but the manuscript does not meet the packet's verbatim memory requirement and contradicts the already-drafted physical memory readers are being asked to recognize.
findings.repair_target: Lines 55-57: recall the warning in Chapter 13's established table/cup setting and preserve the interrupted sentence before 'Don't tell me'; keep the required wording otherwise unchanged.

findings.category: continuity — knowledge of the dead boy's name

draft_evidence.quote: Nobody said anything the boy's crew had not said. That was the rule and nobody had made it; a crew that has just been told a name at a stream-bed does not say it back, and the six had not been told it, and did not ask. The stone went on until it was a shape, and the shape was the size of a boy with a pack too big for him, and then Teague put the last one on, at the head, and stood, and the tall woman picked up the spear.

comparison_evidence.quote:
The broad man, on his face at her knee, with a bolt in his shoulder, said the boy's name.

It was the only time anyone said it. Cael did not enter it. It was not his to enter, and he found — he had not known this about himself either — that there were things he would not write down, and that this was one.

findings.consequence: Cael heard the name spoken in Chapter 21 and consciously chose not to record it; Chapter 22's own closing log also says 'whose name I was told.' Saying the six had not been told it makes the knowledge state contradict both adjacent-chapter evidence and the chapter's log. If the intended distinction is overheard versus formally offered, the current wording does not carry it cleanly.
findings.repair_target: Line 9: preserve the rule that the six do not repeat or claim the name, but reconcile the sentence with the fact that Cael heard it spoken once in the stream-bed.

findings.gate: Packet must_include: mule and boxes recovered by ridge path in one paragraph

draft_evidence.quote:
Lira and Seln went back for the mule.

There was a way. The team had used it: up the shelf's stair, along the ridge above the pass, and down the far side of the hills to the west, where the ground came round to the pass's west mouth from above, and the two of them went that way at Teague's last stone without being asked and came back by dusk, the mule between them with Karis's boxes on it and its head down, having stood tied to a rock all day on the far side of a fall with nothing to say about it, because a mule did not know what had happened on the other side of a heap of stone and a dead tree, and was the only one of the twelve who did not, as it had been the only one on a bridge.

comparison_evidence.quote: The burial at the east mouth in Teague's register; the six carrying stone at his leave; Oryn where she stood; the mule and boxes recovered by the ridge path (one paragraph).

findings.consequence: The recovery itself is correct, but the work order explicitly confines it to one paragraph. The isolated setup gives a logistical bridge beat extra structural weight in a chapter whose promised emphasis is burial and inward reading.
findings.repair_target: Lines 13-15: contain the mule-and-box recovery in one paragraph without expanding the event or changing its route, timing, or participants.

strengths: The burial is emotionally exact and worth protecting. Teague's order, the broad man's one-handed stones, the six carrying only at leave, Oryn's three-stride distance, and the unentered name make grief procedural and physical without gore or consolation.

Worldbuilding is decisively done through mechanism and use. Tide reports absent flow; Rune reports bearer, borne, lean, and structure; the Arbiter is checked like a lamp; cord and brass turn an invisible anomaly into repeatable field evidence. Nothing requires a dossier paragraph.

The non-combat set pieces are memorable. The pass mechanically chooses the burial side, injuries dictate how each person carries stone, firelight prices the Rune reading, and the instrument ritual turns darkness and distance into suspense. There is intentionally no fight, so terrain-caused combat beats and a win sentence of the form 'X removed Y's ability to Z' are not applicable; the chapter does not counterfeit one.

The self-study climax has receipts: the tenth and twelfth remain distinct instruments, Chapter 18's still/set result becomes a deliberate deeper choice, the authorized bones/floor/instruction images arrive in order, and the eyes visibly pay for the knowledge.

The fragment and injury ledger is otherwise exceptionally disciplined. Thirteen remains thirteen; Force recoil stays in the ribs; Teague, Brom, the broad man, Vastin, and Karis all carry the exact physical costs supplied by the previous chapter and state snapshot.

The fixed final log is reproduced with the authorized 'whole year' amendment and ends the file. Its blunt prediction of nothing converts the structural discovery into changed pressure for Chapter 23 without reaching the site early.
concerns: Taste: after the exact permitted finding lands at line 85 ('the same kind of thing, to that instrument, as the sites were to Cleon's'), lines 87-89 explain the same inference again through 'A made thing's inside' and 'He understood what had just happened.' The authorized images keep this short of a verified prohibited reveal, but a human reader should decide whether the second gloss weakens the disciplined boundary the first sentence already holds.

Taste: the chapter leans heavily on the house scaffold 'a man who...' / 'a thing that...' / 'because...' in both burial and analysis. No measured phrase crosses a cap, and the pattern belongs to Cael's voice, but its density occasionally makes distinct emotional and technical beats arrive in the same syntactic register.

Audio/name watch: Cleon and Cael are distinguishable by ear and do not constitute a registry failure, but they occur repeatedly in the same technical paragraphs. A narrator read-through should keep KLEE-on and KAYL sharply separated.
